Mind-Blowing
MYND-bloh-ing
adjective (Boomer slang)
From the phrase blow one’s mind, which entered American slang in the mid-1960s for the effect of a hallucinogenic drug (to shatter one’s ordinary perceptions), and quickly broadened to mean to astonish or overwhelm. Mind-blowing as an adjective is attested from 1967; mind-blower and the shorter mind-blown followed. The Beatles’ "A Day in the Life" (1967) contains "He blew his mind out in a car," a deliberately double-edged line.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Mind-blowing means overwhelming, astonishing, beyond what the mind can take in — and in 1967 it meant, literally, what an LSD trip did to the mind. Grandchildren now say "mind blown" of a magic trick or a science fact. The Christian observation: Scripture is full of the thing this word reaches for, without the chemicals. There is knowledge that genuinely exceeds the human mind, and it is the knowledge of God. David: "Such knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is high, I cannot attain unto it" (Psa 139:6). Paul, at the end of eleven chapters of doctrine, does not conclude; he erupts: "O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!" (Rom 11:33). He prays that believers would "know the love of Christ, which passeth knowledge" (Eph 3:19). The Lord Himself says, "as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways" (Isa 55:9). The difference between that wonder and the drug’s is that God’s overwhelming does not destroy the mind but enlarges it, and it is true. The 1960s sought a mind blown open by chemistry and got confusion. The believer meets a mind lifted by truth and gets worship. If a child is looking for something mind-blowing, open the Gospel to the empty tomb.

Webster 1828 Definition

Boomer slang (1967; from blow one’s mind, of LSD) for astonishing, overwhelming — a wonder Scripture finds in the knowledge of God, too high to attain (Psa 139:6), which enlarges the mind instead of shattering it.

expand to see more

MIND-BLOWING, adj. (Boomer slang, 1967–present) 1. Originally, producing hallucinatory or mind-altering effects, as a drug. 2. Overwhelmingly impressive, astonishing, or surprising. "A mind-blowing concert." Also blow one’s mind (v. phr., mid-1960s); mind-blown (adj., later).

Webster (1828) — BLOW, verb transitive preterit tense blew; participle passive blown. [Latin flo, to blow This word probably is from the same root as bloom, blossom, blow a flower.] 1. To make a current of air; to move as air; as, the wind blows. Often used with it; as, it blows a gale. 2. To pant; to puff; to breathe hard or quick. Here is Mrs. Page at the door, sweating and blowing. 3. To breathe; as, to blow hot and cold.

Decode for families: "mind blown" in a child’s text means "wow." Give them something worth the word.

Key Scripture

Psa 139:6 — "Such knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is high, I cannot attain unto it."

Rom 11:33 — "O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!"

Eph 3:19 — "And to know the love of Christ, which passeth knowledge, that ye might be filled with all the fulness of God."

Isa 55:9 — "For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways, and my thoughts than your thoughts."

1Co 2:9 — "But as it is written, Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God hath prepared for them that love him."

Modern Corruption

The 1960s sought an overwhelmed mind through drugs and called it revelation; Scripture offers the true overwhelming — the depth of the riches of God — which ends not in confusion but in doxology.

expand to see more

The phrase began as a description of damage. To blow the mind was to break its ordinary operation, and the drug culture prized the breakage as a doorway. Wonder was confused with derangement. That confusion is still with us whenever astonishment is sought as a sensation for its own sake — the next bigger spectacle, the next louder concert, the next more shocking fact.

Scripture keeps wonder tethered to truth. Paul’s "O the depth" (Rom 11:33) comes after careful argument, not instead of it. The wonder rises out of understanding and runs beyond it. "Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God hath prepared for them that love him" (1Co 2:9). That is the only genuinely mind-blowing sentence, because it is about the only thing too big for every mind — and true.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English myne / gemynd (mind) + Old English bláwan (to blow) → mid-1960s blow one’s mind (of LSD) → 1967 adj. mind-blowing.

expand to see more

Old English gemynd — memory, thought, the mind

Old English bláwan — to blow, as wind; later, to burst or shatter

Mid-1960s: blow one’s mind — to undergo or cause a hallucinogenic experience; to astonish

1967: mind-blowing, adj.; later mind-blower, mind-blown

Scripture: Psa 139:6; Rom 11:33 — knowledge too wonderful to attain

Usage

""Grandma thought the moon landing was mind-blowing. She was right.""

"O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! (Rom 11:33)."

"The love of Christ passeth knowledge (Eph 3:19) — the wonder that enlarges the mind."
